speakeroldname: Mr. Albert Cooper (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 36(8), I have the honour to table, in both official languages, the government's response to 10 petitions.
[Editor's Note: See today's Votes and Proceedings.]

Madam Speaker, I have a very lengthy petition here.
The petition is signed by citizens of Canada from Huntsville, Barrys Bay, Ontario, Pembroke, Renfrew, Combermere, Whitney, Highland Grove and many other places throughout Ontario.
This petition is to draw to the attention of the House that mace and tear gas canisters are illegal in Canada because they infringe on the rights of the perpetrator. These canisters can be lifesavers to our female population when rape and murder of these people is on a dramatic increase.
Therefore, your petitioners call upon Parliament to legalize mace and tear gas canisters in Canada for self-protection.

Madam Speaker, I have the honour to present a petition
signed by about 150 people from southern Saskatchewan, including the communities of Assiniboia and Gravel-bourg.
These people have observed what is happening to the rural way of life and have said enough is enough especially when it comes to the closure of rural post offices.
Therefore, the petitioners are calling on Parliament to support Canada's rural way of life, to support the maintenance of rural post offices and postal services and to reject this government's agenda of cutbacks and closures.

Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to present a petition on behalf of a number of constituents from Kamloops, British Columbia.
The petitioners are concerned about the potential of cutbacks in the RCMP. They are asking that the government ensure that proper funding for the RCMP is maintained to enable it to fulfil its mandate and role as the only police force for communities across British Columbia. It is a viable symbol of Canadian unity at this critical time.

Madam Speaker, on another matter, the petitioners who again reside primarily in communities throughout British Columbia point out their concern about an intention to divert one of the British Columbia rivers to service the California area in the United States.
The petitioners are asking that the government not allow this river to be dammed or diverted into the United States.

Madam Speaker, I too have the honour to present another petition certified as to form and content by the Clerk. It has been signed by a couple of hundred people in the Middleton, Annapolis and Digby area.

Government Orders
The petitioners show a concern with the direction the Department of National Defence has taken in terms of its defence policy particularly as it relates to Canadian Forces Base Cornwallis. They want to continue the recruit training but want to see additional jobs kept there in terms of where the policy for national defence is going.
They would like to see a new direction by national defence to increase the use at CFB Cornwallis and particularly perhaps even put a peacekeeping training centre at CFB Cornwallis.

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I will not take a great deal of the time of the House today for debate on third reading of Bill C-18.
I might point out that my colleague from the New Democratic Party was intending to ask for unanimous consent to introduce an amendment which I can tell the House we would have opposed. This was not because of the amendment but because of its late arrival and not having had the opportunity to examine it.
However I have given him a commitment on behalf of the Minister of Finance that we will look at his proposal very carefully and give it consideration in the next technical bill that comes from finance at a later date.
Before I get into covering the items in the bill I want to thank the finance committee and all those who participated in the consideration of this bill and others.
December 5, 1991

Madam Speaker, in this fall session those involved in the finance committee, as well as legislative committees dealing with finance matters, have done a great deal of work in committee. There has been good discussion and great co-operation among the parties. I think that unfortunately the public from time to time bases its views on the proceedings here in the House of Commons during Question Period. That may not be the best place for people to understand what goes on in this place and in the other place as well. I appeared before the Senate last night. The work that goes on in committee and in debates in this House, other than Question Period, is most productive under most circumstances.
The work that has been done this fall with the finance and legislative committees dealing with financial matters has been tremendous. That is my area of concern as you know, Madam Speaker, so I can only comment on that. I know other work has gone on but the work has been tremendous and I just want to at this time publicly thank all those who have been associated with it.
A fair and efficient tax system plays a very vital role in creating the stability that we require for growth and prosperity. The goals of equity and efficiency are at the heart of the various measures of tax reform the government has introduced as part of the agenda for economic renewal that we set out back in 1984.
Bill C-18 will help to improve the fairness and efficiency of our tax system to the advantage of Canadians in a number of important areas. The scope of the bill alone I believe testifies to that.
This bill includes Bmeasures that were announced in both the 1990 and 1991 budgets and incorporates a number of initiatives that were announced separately from these budgets. It embodies a number of amendments, mainly technical in nature, that are directed to improving administrative fairness of the tax system.
I should also acknowledge the useful guidance we have received on the technical aspects of the bill through consultations with taxpayers and their advisers. Since the measures were announced the Department of Finance has conducted extensive consultations on them and they were improved as a result of this process.
Government Orders
As I have suggested, Bill C-18 encompasses measures to improve the fairness of the tax system in a number of important areas. I would like to go over them quickly if I may just for a few minutes.
The Canadian tax system has long recognized an obligation to promote equality in its treatment of Canadians with physical and mental disabilities and those who are not disabled. Bill C-18 gives effect to a number of measures to improve and to broaden tax assistance for disabled Canadians. These measures were announced in the February 1991 budget by my colleague the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and International Trade. He was then the Minister of Finance. I will not go into all of them today but I would like to highlight just a couple.
The disability tax credit will be increased in 1991 by $125 to $700. The criteria for eligibility for this tax credit will be clarified to ensure greater fairness and uniformity in its application. This will increase federal assistance to disabled Canadians by $35 million a year.
The medical tax credit will be broadened for the disabled. The list of medical expenses that are eligible for the credit is expanded and non-working Canadians with disabilities will receive a credit for part-time attendant care.
The owners of buildings who undertake renovations to improve access to the disabled will be able to deduct the cost of such renovations immediately rather than over a number of years. Of course we see these renovations going on. There is more to be done. And we would encourage people whose facilities have not been converted to accommodate the disabled to do so. We believe this tax measure will go a long way in helping that to come about.
Taken together with the other changes, Madam Speaker, these measures represent a significant advance in the way the tax system promotes equal opportunities for Canadians with disabilities. The Minister of Finance and I have been conducting pre-budget consultations across the country. We met just last week in Toronto with members of the Canadian Paraplegic Association who were very quick to draw to our attention that there are further things the federal government can do to improve the lot of the disabled. We accepted their representations. They were articulately presented. Of course we are taking a look on an ongoing basis at these represen-

Government Orders
tations to see where we can in fact improve the fairness of the system for those with disabilities.
Bill C-18 also includes measures from the 1990 and 1991 budgets which are designed to strengthen Canadian culture. A very, very important part of being a Canadian is our Canadian culture.
This is something the government for a very long time has looked into, to see how we can improve the situation of artists and artisans in our country to assure they are properly recognized and treated fairly within our tax system.
The Income Thx Act encourages gifts of cultural property to certain Canadian institutions or public authorities by providing special tax treatment for such donations. Some artists donate their works and we want to assure that Bill C-18 covers the streamlining of the rules of governing cultural donations by enhancing the role of the Canadian Cultural Property Export Review Board in assessing the value of such property.
There are also measures in this bill that will benefit artists directly. Artists who are employed will now be allowed to claim a deduction for expenses incurred in the exercise of their artistic employment. A self-employed artist who donates certified works to designated institutions or public authorities will be allowed to claim a charitable tax credit without having the value of those works included in income. These all come from representations made over the past number of years by artists in Canada and a commitment by the Prime Minister to assure that changes are made so that our artists are recognized. I do not believe any sector of our economy has played a more important role.
I want to now return to the sector of small business. I think there is no sector in our economy that has played a more vital role in creating growth and new jobs than the small business sector. Bill C-18 includes two measures reflecting the government's commitment to encouraging investment in small business enterprises.
The first is an improvement in the tax treatment of small business share holdings. The reason for it is because a taxpayer who realizes a capital gain on the disposition of shares of a qualifying small business corporation is eligible for an enhanced capital gains
exemption of $500,000. When a successful private corporation wants to expand by having its shares listed on a Canadian stock exchange, it ceases to be a qualifying small business corporation. The result is that the enhanced capital gains exemption will no longer be available to the original shareholders even in respect of gains that accrued while the corporation did qualify for the exemption. The situation penalizes successful businesses.
Bill C-18 remedies this anomaly by allowing a small business to go public without sacrificing its shareholders' enhanced exemption. That makes abundant sense.
A second initiative that will be helpful to small business concerns is new rules relating to national labour sponsored venture capital corporations. These will encourage investment in small and developing businesses. If we have heard anything in the pre-budget representations of a common theme coming from all the associations and groups that we are meeting, it is the problem of venture capital in this country.
Our pre-budget consultations are being done a little differently this year in that we are doing it with groups altogether rather than one on one. We are meeting with groups together and they are talking to one another, which is wonderful. The National Action Committee sat in on meetings with the Canadian Bankers Association and the Retail Council of Canada and the agricultural community. They started talking to one another and understood that they had mutual problems and concerns.
When we got talking about the issue of venture capital, the theme was that we need venture capital in this country, but the solutions of how to handle the venture capital, encourage venture capital, came from three different groups, all with different ideas, all opposing the other person's idea because it would not work for this reason or for that reason.
What transpired out of this meeting was that these groups decided to get together to try and come up with a consistent presentation that they feel would work in this country to encourage venture capital. We believe that these meetings are being successful. They are being well attended, we are getting very good comments on them afterward, and the participation has been phenomenal. I

just spoke to the Minister of Finance who is out west now. He had one just the last day in Winnipeg.
He said it was a great success. There was great conversation, groups were talking to one another and realizing we are all in this together. We all have common interests and we should all work together for the common good.
I am quite excited about the concept. After sitting in on the first two, being a doubting Thomas at the beginning of the process, I have been converted. It has been a great consultative process and one that will bring benefits to our country.
The key element to the government's approach is to ensure that all income in Canada is fairly taxed. A number of initiatives brought together in Bill C-18 are directed toward that goal, including measures relating to taxation of non-residents, life insurers and registered education savings plans. I will touch very briefly on each of these.
In the 1990 budget there were measures announced to ensure that non-residents who deal in Canadian real estate or who create mutual funds to invest in Canadian real estate are taxed appropriately. This bill also extends the tax on financial institutions introduced as part of tax reform to large life insurance companies.
There is also a refinement in rules related to registered educations savings plans. It will limit the total amount that may be contributed in respect to each beneficiary and will allow the payment of benefits to a beneficiary under a new plan only if he or she is a full-time student. These amendments with other related changes will improve control over the plans.
Other important amendments revise the system of tax benefits for residents of Canada's northern and isolated regions, simplify the computation of the investment income tax paid by life insurance companies, and implement what are known as the available for-use rules for the timing of certain expenses and credits.
This bill also touches on pension funds. This measure recognizes the advantages of investment diversification of pension funds. Before 1990 pension funds were subject to a special tax if more than 10 per cent of the assets consisted of foreign property. Bill C-18 includes
Government Orders
the proposal announced in the 1990 budget to allow pension funds to invest up to 20 per cent of the assets in foreign property by 1994.
From an administrative point of view, from the perspective of the individual taxpayer, Bill C-18 represents a step forward by improving the administrative fairness and responsiveness of the tax system. It gives the Minister of National Revenue a discretion to this end in a number of areas.
For example, if a taxpayer discovers after the normal reassessment period has expired that he or she has inadvertently failed to claim a deduction, the Minister of National Revenue will be able to adjust the amount of tax paid for and refund any overpayment. The minister will also have the discretion to waive penalties in interest where an individual has failed to comply with the law due to extraordinary circumstances such as a natural disaster or a serious illness.
This is another area I run into all the time, especially with small businesses in which the person runs the business, does the books, et cetera. They may have missed a payment to Revenue Canada for a veiy legitimate reason. Automatically they get a late payment penalty, interest charges and so on. There have been extenuating circumstances to waive those. We believe this is very important especially for small businesses. The large businesses have their systems in place, it is not a problem for them. It is usually the little guy who has those problems. This will help him.
I am not encouraging people not to make their payments on time. There have to be legitimate reasons for it and there are.
Finally, this bill contains a number of technical amendments that provide relief for taxpayers in other unanticipated situations in which the existing law would operate inappropriately. Others are intended to ensure the internal consistency of the tax system or clarify ambiguous provisions.
All of these measures reflect the government's continuing concern that the Canadian tax system should be as fair and as efficient as any in the world.
For that reason Bill C-18 deserves the support of this House. Again I want to thank colleagues from all sides of the House for their work on this bill and for their co-operation.

December 5, 1991
Government Orders

Madam Speaker, the bill before us today is a complex piece of legislation in line with the complexity of the subject itself.
One only need lift the bill to see the weight of the proposals in it. It numbers some 2,000 pages and it deals, as the minister has just said in his introductory statement for third reading, with a variety of measures.
We in the Official Opposition support most of these measures without reservation. They correct anomalies and unintended results in the tax system.
Certainly the measures benefiting artists, the establishment of tax regulation of international shipping corporations with their headquarters in Canada, the penalty for large corporations and the replacement property rule are areas which we had the opportunity to discuss at some considerable length in committee.
The final results are satisfactory to us. I want to say, however, that when the minister speaks of this bill in some way reflecting tax reform, I find that a rather large claim to make for what is essentially a technical bill.
As my colleague from Broadview-Greenwood will no doubt expand on in a few minutes, this bill does not deal with tax fairness. To claim that this is in some broad sense a measure of the government's commitment to tax fairness is to miss the point altogether.
My colleague from Ottawa South in the House on October 7 had the opportunity to deal at some length with the questions of tax fairness, an issue which has increased among Canadians as they recognize the growing impact of the Tories' tax policies on them and on the corporations of Canada with regard to their international competitiveness.
My colleague from Broadview-Greenwood has brought forward a number of suggestions with regard to tax simplification which are worthy of serious consideration. I am sure he will want to develop some of those ideas in his intervention, and so I will not spend time on that question at the moment.
I do however want to say that the member for Ottawa South in his very able intervention of more than a month ago pointed out the fact that tax reform is obviously a very complex matter. It raises questions of fairness.
The government set a goal when it came to office back in 1984 to establish a greater degree of fairness in the tax system. The result is nothing of the sort. We do not have a fairer tax system in Canada.
We still have a situation in which higher income individuals and profitable corporations are not carrying by any means what would be regarded as a fair proportion of the total tax load.
The fact the tax load is grossly inflated, that is to say far too high, is another question which I will deal with in a moment. In terms of tax fairness, one would wonder about the equity of the system introduced by the Conservative government when the progress of the tax system has been reduced. The resort to sales taxes as opposed to income taxes has inevitably reduced that progressivity in our tax system and imposed yet a higher burden on the individual Canadian.
Let me say in that context too that the tax treatment of families in our society has to be a matter of real concern to all Canadians, and indeed I think to members of this House when they address questions on the tax system.
I would suggest that certainly nothing in this bill and indeed nothing in the government's agenda would indicate fundamental reform of the tax system so as to provide for a more equitable treatment of families, which seems to me an essential element in any reformed tax system. I regret the government did not take this opportunity or any other opportunity-I hope it might in the forthcoming budget but we will see about that-to address itself to the question of the equitable treatment of families in our society with regard to taxation.
I have touched in a few questions with regard to fairness and equity in our tax system, but I would leave it for some of my other colleagues to develop some of those ideas at greater length in response to the minister's statement that this bill introduces a greater measure of fairness into the tax system. Any Canadian would wonder very much about fairness in the tax system when they have experienced constant increases in the levels of taxation in Canada since this government first came to office.

At the root of our economic difficulties and in a sense behind this bill today is the fact that Canadians have consistently consumed more over the past decades than they have invested or even produced. Much of this consumption has been fuelled by the federal government which consistently has failed to follow a counter cyclical fiscal policy.
The minister who just introduced the bill will know very well that when this government came to office in 1984 and in the years following when it benefited from the growing prosperity of our economy as the result of measures introduced by the previous government in 1982-1983, it did not take that occasion to act as it had promised the Canadian people, to restrict government spending, to ensure that government spending was targeted to those it was intended to benefit. Instead it continued throughout a period of unparalleled prosperity in Canada to spend and spend freely, contributing thereby to a constantly growing deficit and a constantly growing debt.
The fact is that after seven years in office this government will leave the Canadian people with a legacy of a yet higher debt and a yet higher deficit. All of us know every well that this year we will see the government has been unable to live up to its forecasts. It will not be able to meet its planned restrictions on deficit spending, and what will the result be?
The fact is that the deficit spending of the government has drained much needed private savings from our economy. There is a sort of crowding out effect. The government is borrowing on the capital markets and seeking the capital which would have otherwise been utilized by private investment, thereby improving productivity in Canada and our international competitiveness instead of being used to finance public overconsumption. One result of this has been that private investors and provincial governments, for that matter, have had to seek capital offshore, thereby driving up through their foreign borrowing, Canada's foreign indebtedness.
At the same time the government, having failed and failed completely-let us not fool ourselves about that- to deal with the question of the deficit and debt, has too engaged in offshore borrowing. Canada's foreign indebtedness now stands at record heights. The fact is that Canadians are building up a problem they will have to deal with in years ahead but deal with in a way that will be painful and difficult.
Government Orders
I would draw attention to what happens when the government seeks to finance its excessive spending through foreign borrowing. One thing we get is higher interest rates. Higher interest rates do not result only from foreign borrowing but they certainly contribute to foreign borrowing. We drive up interest rates for the purpose of attracting foreign capital. The result is that the Canadian dollar follows along in most instances and the Canadian dollar is then placed at a substantially greater level than its real value and certainly above a level optimal for Canada's exports. As a result Canada is haemorrhaging capital at the same time that our exports are being priced out of world markets
I said a moment ago that the federal government has been living beyond its mean. To be fair, I think one would have to say that Canadians have been living beyond their means. However, instead of making things better, this government has continuously pursued the wrong mix of economic policies. It has unbalanced our economy even further and compounded both our domestic and international debt problems.
The combination of a tight monetary policy, a deliberate overvaluation of the Canadian dollar, the large government deficits which this government has not tackled in any effective manner, and the lack of any industrial strategy, have created the economic mess that Canada is in today.
When I speak of an economic strategy I have no intention of suggesting that this government should have pursued a winner's and loser's policy of attempting massive intervention in the economy to attempt to control every last detail of our economy, but rather that it should pursue those elements of public policy that can contribute to our international competitiveness.
I say that for two reasons. One reason is that Canada in the short run is going to be able to pay off its growing and worrisome foreign indebtedness which this government has incurred by exporting. There is no other way to do it. We must export to pay off our foreign debts. How is this government going to engage in exports? It is only going to be able to do so by helping to render Canadians more competitive.
Underneath that there is yet another issue. The fact is that this government knows very well that international competitiveness for Canada, for Canadians, has become the only way in which we can match and counter the effects of globalization in investment and trade. Globalization is a problem confronting every country. Some of

Government Orders
course are dealing with the question effectively. Others such as Canada have faltered and been hesitant about how to deal with this growing phenomenon of the mobility of labour, capital and goods across the world. I say "labour" in the sense of being able to manufacture in any jurisdiction.
What has this government done? What we have seen in the past month or so is a proposal for 12 more months of consultation. Twelve months to decide what? After seven years of do-nothing policies, this government has suddenly decided the thing it must do is take another year to ask Canadian people whether they think our education system is adequate.
Is there anyone in Canada who thinks our education system is adequate? Is there any doubt in anyone's mind? Come to my constituency or that of the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands and the people will tell you that they are dissatisfied with their education system. They know they are taxed heavily to pay for it. They know, as does my colleague from High Park who is a teacher and a distinguished school principal, that the system of education in this country is seen not only as lacking substance in itself, but rendering Canadians incapable of competing effectively in the global economy, which I described just a moment ago.
Not only has the government decided to postpone any of the decisions that might contribute in a sense on a micro-economic level to helping Canadians compete and thereby win that higher standard of living which we all see, but on the macro-economic side this government has failed as well. On the macro-economic side we see the government having become preoccupied, to put it kindly, with a monetary policy that uses interest rates as the single weapon in the government's armoury against inflation.
This is a gross distortion of government policy. The government has more tools at its disposal than merely high interest rates. The result is that we get, in the name of fighting inflation, an economy which is incapable of competing effectively abroad. We suffer from very high tax rates. We suffer from the lack of government
involvement in rendering the economy more efficient, in creating a framework for Canadians to help themselves and the result is that we have what I called an economic mess earlier, an unbalanced economy, the wrong mix of economic policies.
If this government had pursued a balanced economic policy, that is one that used fiscal tools, restrained its own spending, as well as a moderate policy of monetary intervention, I think we would be in a much better economic position. Those who are unemployed, those who are at the food banks of Canada and those who see little future for their children would not suffer from the very real concerns that inflict them today.
With that comment on the bill and on the thinking behind the bill, I shall conclude simply by saying that although we intend to support this bill, I want it to be placed on record that the economic policies which this government has followed in part created the circumstances where this bill was necessary. They have been the wrong policies and misguided policies. This government must change them or certainly the next government will.

Madam Speaker, I will begin by saying that it is always interesting to listen to the hon. member from Etobicoke because he has a history of speaking on behalf of the real Liberal Party as opposed to the Liberal Party that we see represented in the rhetoric of Question Period when the various cuts that the government has made in government spending have been criticized vociferously by the Liberal opposition. The member then gets up and says that one of the things that the government has not done enough of is to cut government spending and be fiscally responsible. It has always been a great mystery to me, and I am sure to a great many other Canadians, just who speaks for the Liberal Party. Perhaps I will have time to deal with that in greater detail later on.
First of all, having to do with what the minister said at the beginning of his remarks, there was an amendment suggested to clause 91 of this bill by the Canadian Association for Community Living, which would have addressed a flaw in Bill C-18 having to do with the mentally handicapped vis-a-vis the disability tax credit.
December 5, 1991

The hon. member for Beaches-Woodbine will, I think, have more to say about that when he rises to participate in this debate, but I want to thank the minister for his commitment to consider this amendment.
This problem was brought to the attention of the committee and to the attention of the House by Mr. Paul Badertscher who appeared before the committee in this respect. He had suggested an amendment which in turn prompted the Canadian Association for Community Living to suggest its own amendment, an amendment for which we had hoped might receive unanimous consent to be put before the House here at report stage, but the government indicated that it did not feel it had had sufficient time to study the amendment. We hope that in the next round of technical amendments, as the minister said, that this problem will be dealt with.
This bill is an omnibus bill and omnibus bills always present problems for the opposition because invariably there are things in the bill that you support. In this case there are a great many things, technical amendments, housekeeping amendments, changes of language for instance to eliminate exclusive language and to use inclusive language, et cetera. A lot of these things are to some extent value-neutral, although many of the housekeeping amendments so-called are housekeeping amendments to tax measures which we have criticized in the past. Then, of course, there are things in the bill to which we take offence. So we will not be able to give our support to the bill in that context.
For instance, just to return to the question of disabled Canadians, the disability tax credit has increased from $575 to $700 per year, which obviously is a welcome change to the tax system. But the claw-back formula indexed to inflation only above 3 per cent per year is being placed on it. Surely the needs of the disabled do not increase by only the amount of inflation above 3 per cent. So we find, even in a good measure, the ambiguity of including a measure which we oppose across the board, whether we find it applied to family allowances or the disability tax credit or any other place where the government seeks to limit its responsibility to make sure that the social policy commitments that it has made in the past keep their value and continue to do so for these targeted groups of Canadians, whether they be families, the disabled or other groups, what the original policy decision intended.
Government Orders
Instead, we have built into a number of these social policy commitments a recipe for eventual irrelevance, in terms of monetary significance, if this formula having to do with the claw-back continues to be built in to the government's social policy commitments.
Another thing which interested us in this bill was the whole question of northern tax benefits. I think the hon. member for Prince George-Bulkley Valley will be addressing that on behalf of the NDP caucus.
Over all, this bill does not address, as the member before said, tax fairness. Surely anybody who has bothered to read the bill realizes that there is nothing in this bill which so substantially transforms the Canadian income tax system that it could be called an attempt at tax fairness or anything like it. The fact is that those elements of the Canadian income tax system which are unfair have not been addressed in this particular bill. In fact, over the life of this government the tax system in this country has become increasingly unfair.
It was not an absolutely perfect system that the government inherited in 1984 when it took over. Let us not kid ourselves. There were many inequities built into it, many tax shelters, loopholes, et cetera, tax expenditures that had been put in there by the previous Liberal government, a great many of them in the 1970s. Some of these have been eliminated but in our judgment some of the big ones have yet to be touched by this government, while at the same time it has increased the burden on middle class Canadians.
I think the icing on the cake is of course the GST which has been harder on middle class Canadians than on anyone else. I think that what we are seeing in this country is a growing sense of tax aversion, that people are feeling taxed to death. This leads to all kinds of regrettable political and ideological consequences in the sense that people are being conditioned through an increased tax load to accept the notion that some of the social programs that we have in this country need to be scaled down, diminished or cut back in some way, when in fact if we bothered to look at it in an analytical way, we find for instance a study that was done through Statistics Canada which shows that it is not social programs that are causing the deficit. It is tax expenditures, the interest rate being paid on the debt. These kinds of things are-

Government Orders
What is Bob Rae doing about it? Tell us about Bob Rae and his silk stockings.

I am not sure what the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands is saying. I cannot hear him. Is he disagreeing? I take it the Liberals are disagreeing with my claim that it is not social programs that are the cause of the deficit.
Everything is causing the deficit.

He says everything is the cause of the deficit. To simply say everything is the cause of the deficit is not to be too discriminating in nature. Perhaps that is the line that the Liberals would like to take now after their thinkers' conference. It is almost a contradiction to think about a Liberal thinkers' conference.
Nevertheless, they had a conference at which they came out and finally revealed their true colours, the colours revealed by the hon. member from Etobicoke here when he spoke on behalf of the real Liberal Party: i.e. globalization is something that we have to accept and accommodate ourselves to, protectionism is passe, the Liberal argument against the free trade agreement is now proving to have been as phoney as we thought it was in 1988. They have accepted the North American free trade agreement idea. Just the other day a Liberal member of the legislature in Manitoba proposed a motion having to do with the North American free trade agreement which basically accepted the reality of those negotiations and simply asked that something be done about labour and environmental standards.
We see here the true face of the Liberal Party which is committed to the same corporate world view, to the same corporate agenda as the Conservative Party. Why should we be surprised about that? We know that the Liberal Party and the Conservative Party are funded by the same people. The same piper calls the tune. The Liberal Party is permitted to sound progressive at election time, if that means that somehow progressive Canadians can be tricked into voting Liberal.
When it comes to the tax system, let us remember that most of the unfairness built into the tax system, particularly through tax expenditures, was built into the tax system in the 1970s by Liberal governments. We still do not hear the Liberal Party collectively calling for the elimination of those tax loopholes. There might be the odd individual, like the hon. member for Broadview-
Greenwood, who wants to replace the whole system with a flat tax, or single tax. Fair enough. I do not agree with him but at least he has an idea about what to do with the tax system.
But I very carefully said I have never heard the Liberal Party collectively, because the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood is not the tax critic for his party, as much as he might like to be. The hon. member for Ottawa South is the tax critic for his party and he has not, on behalf of the Liberal Party, called for the elimination of these loopholes.
The tax system cannot solve the deficit problem by itself without changes in monetary and fiscal policy like lower interest rates. But much could be done if there was the political will to eliminate significant tax expenditures.
For example, the present tax system allows business people to deduct 80 per cent of the cost of all their business meals and entertainment, including GST. This cost the federal government over $1 billion in tax revenue, exactly the amount that was withdrawn from federal support for medicare in the 1991 budget.
When asked about this bias in favour of lunches over nurses, the finance minister talks about competitiveness with the United States. This is the famous level playing field we were promised. We level our health care system down-some would say level it completely-and are unable to make the tough-minded tax choices that we should be making in the current situation. If Canadian business depends on this tax expenditure for its very survival, we are indeed in sorry shape.
While Canadians are lining up at food banks, taxpayers should not be financing and encouraging the over-consumption of entertainment at the expense of productive investment through this particular business tax deduction.
The manufacturing and processing tax credit was introduced in the early 1970s to combat a subsidy that the U.S. provided for American exporters. In 1986 the American government repealed the tax subsidy but Canada did not repeal the manufacturing and tax processing credit. This tax credit's continued existence was justified as a way of off-setting the despised manufacturers' sales tax.

The MST has now been replaced by the GST, but this $1 billion annual tax expenditure survived the budget and in the House of Commons on February 27, the then Minister of Finance, the Minister for International Trade, defended it as if no changes had occurred in Canada or the United States.
The lifetime capital gains exemption when it was established at $500,000 in the 1985 budget brought the entire Tory caucus to its feet in one of the longest and most ecstatic standing ovations ever seen in the middle of a budget speech. I was there, Madam Speaker, and I remember it well.
In 1987 this cheering was no doubt echoed by the wealthiest 10 per cent of Canadians who received over 80 per cent of this non-taxed form of income. This provision has since been moderated. It continues to cost the Treasury about $1.7 billion a year, revenue forgone that must be replaced by sacrifices on the part of lower and middle income Canadians.
The dividend tax credit cost the government about $1 billion each year. The original justification for this measure was to avoid double taxation by compensating shareholders for part of the corporate tax paid and to encourage Canadians to invest in Canadian shares.
Given the number of corporations that manage to pay no taxes at all, this attempt to prevent double taxation often amounts to a guarantee of no taxation. At the same time there is scant evidence that the other economic goals of this tax expenditure are being realized at all.
Other tax expenditures like the subsidies given to real estate developers by which they claim depreciation on property that is actually increasing in value, the subsidy given to the corporate world through deductions for advocacy advertising, the endless deferral of corporate taxes by exaggerated depreciation of capital assets, the abuse of the interest deductibility rule for purposes other than stimulating small businesses, all add up to a truly astounding amount of money that can be called nothing other than a hidden form of government spending.
The billions of dollars spent through tax expenditures is the hidden reality behind the big lie that it is social spending. That is the cause of the deficit. It is interest on the debt, aggravated by a self-inflicted policy of high interest rates, in combination with the cumulative effect
Government Orders
of the tax expenditure spending by successive governments that is the cause of the deficit.
The removal of the tax expenditures in question, complemented by a more progressive income tax system, particularly at the top end where now no distinction exists between the marginal rates for people earning $60,000 and those who make $600,000, and some form of wealth tax would provide billions for the Canadian government to reduce the deficit and spend on the things that would make a country truly competitive.
We are constantly being presented by the Tories with the false dilemma of having to choose between social justice and being competitive. The truth is that taxes are only one factor among many that make a country attractive as a place to invest as well as to live.
The Conservatives are making the fatal mistake of choosing what might be called negative competitiveness, sacrificing social harmony, important infrastructure, research and development and Canada's human and ecological capital, when a truly wise government would collect taxes in a fair and equitable way and invest the revenue in the things that would count for positive competitiveness in the 21st century.
Those who leave such a Canada, who would carry through on their threat to go elsewhere if we were to introduce this kind of fair tax system because they object to fair taxes spent wisely and justly will come back as so many doctors did in the 1970s from the U.S. where they discovered that a high income is not all there is to practising good medicine. Or, are we better off without them? At a time when Canadians are to be united about anything, it should be by a common quest for social justice.
Madam Speaker, if I have any time left, I would like to expand on this notion of positive competitiveness because there is more than one way to be competitive.
The problem with the free trade agreement and with the North American free trade agreement, if that it comes through, is that it will be a beggar thy neighbour kind of competitiveness: who can get down to the lowest wages, the weakest environmental regulations, the most despicable labour standards or whatever the case maybe.

December 5, 1991
Government Orders
Now states like Georgia, et cetera are advertising: "Come down and invest here. We do not have any of those horrible kinds of regulations they have up there in Canada where you have to pay people a decent wage and respect the environment". It is not that we respect it all that much up here, Madam Speaker, but perhaps we respect it more than they do in Georgia. It will get even worse under an agreement with Mexico.
The other way to compete, Madam Speaker, is to compete the way that some other countries in the world do it like Germany, Japan, Sweden and many other countries where you say: "We are going to have the kind of research and development, we are going to have the kind of transportation and telecommunications infrastructure, we are going to have the kind of trained work force, et cetera that is going to make this a good place to invest regardless of the fact that we may have higher taxes and expensive social programs".
That is not the way this government is going. It is not the way North America is going. I regret it. It is a kind of vicious cycle that we get into instead of what economist Robert Reich, for instance, has suggested is the kind of virtuous cycle that we should get into, building upon our strengths, building to be competitive rather than dismantling to be competitive which is exactly the kind of competitive atmosphere that we have ourselves into now.

Madam Speaker, first, before I ask my hon. friend from Winnipeg Transcona a question, I would like to clear up some of his assertions.
He made a comment concerning my colleague, the member for Etobicoke North. The hon. member is accurately reflecting the spirit that exists within the Liberal Party right now, that is, one where we are debating all sides of these very complex issues.
We are not too concerned about the fact that he is debating complex issues from time to time. It is natural that we seem to have in the spirit of honest debate slight differences of opinion. I want to clarify his point about the Aylmer Liberal think-tank conference.
The hon. member should know that this was not a Liberal think-tank conference. It was organized through the initiative of a couple of keen Liberals but in fact we had people there speaking to some members of our caucus and other members of our party at large.
The speakers were in fact mostly non-Liberal. We opened our party up to the views of New Democrats who were present there, to Conservatives and to people from all over the world because we were trying to clarify some of the complex issues that we as national politicians are facing today.
The thing that disturbed me a little bit were the member's assertions about our history as Liberals in contributing to the complexity of the tax system. I think we as Liberals have toB accept some of that fault and I believe most would. However, he is being rather unfair because he is forgetting that his New Democratic friend Premier Rae during the last election ran on a campaign of fair taxation in the province of Ontario. I thought he did the right thing by making that a central issue in his campaign.
However, since he has come to power, like the Conservatives, he basically has only set up a fair taxation commission. In the process of his attempt to tiy and do something constructive, he has so frightened the investment community in regard to his approach that the flight of capital, specifically in the province of Ontario, has been reduced in the last year by almost 50 per cent.
My question to the hon. member is quite simple. Does he not realize that attracting foreign capital to this country is essential for job creation? It is absolutely essential for job creation, in my opinion. Does he not realize that attracting foreign capital must be done through the tax system? I would just like to have his remarks on that.

Madam Speaker, perhaps the member himself or somebody on behalf of the Liberals could say what they mean by attracting foreign capital through the tax systems. If this means making Canada some kind of tax haven where people can come here and make money and not contribute to the country, then I am not interested in that kind of capital attraction policy.
You mentioned the Government of Ontario. Again, with respect, you are trying to have it both ways. It is ludicrous to compare the policies of the Ontario NDP government with the policies of this government. This government has gone to great pains to say how much it is different from and opposed to and against the policies of the Ontario government. The Ontario government is constantly being vilified by this government for following

an entirely different economic policy with respect to the deficit, et cetera.
With respect to taxes the member has said that it has established this fair tax commission. Nothing has happened, because the commission has not reported yet. The member is saying: "How come we have not acted", and at the same time is saying: "The very fact that they even established the notion of fair taxes is driving capital out of the province of Ontario". Which is it? Are you saying that it should have established a fair tax system earlier and, according to your analysis, driven more capital out of Ontario?
The problem is, as the hon. member knows or maybe did not have time to say or is not willing to admit, that the problem in Ontario is not related so much to the NDP government or to anything happening with respect to domestic policy. It is related to the free trade agreement.
It is the awful misfortune of the NDP government to be elected just at the time when the effects of the FTA are kicking in, in Ontario. If the Liberals are telling me that they do not think it is the FTA that is wrecking the Ontario economy, I wish they would get up and say so. If that is an analysis they reject, I would like to know it and I would like to see it on the record. The fact is that it is the FTA.
When I hear members of the provincial Government of Ontario talking about the recession, I say it is not just the recession. It is not like any other recession. It is the North American continental economy kicking in, in a way that Ontario will never recover from regardless of whatever policies any provincial government ever has, unless we find a way to extricate ourselves from the free trade agreement and from the upcoming North American free trade agreement.

Madam Speaker, I have a few questions for the hon. member of the New Democratic Party.
It is said that capital is leaving Canada, that business people are moving to the United States and that there is a brain drain toward the United States. It is said that about 50 per cent of our university graduates and qualified technicians are moving to the United States. This means we are training them for the benefit of the
Government Orders
U.S. The main reason is, of course, that in the United States they pay 25 per cent less income tax than we pay here in Canada.
Unfortunately people move to the United States because they will have 25 per cent more disposable income. Some people say the socialist system is efficient and satisfactory, but I think we are going bankrupt with all this, and the statistics are there to prove it. Two weeks ago the statistics were right there in the media to prove it.
So the reason is clear. A study prepared by a consulting firm in Montreal said that in the United States a person who earns $100,000 and pays for exactly the same services we get in Canada or Quebec-and especially in Quebec, because the study was made for Quebec- whether we are talking about medical care or anything else, that person has $25,000 more left in disposable income. That is how the system works, and if the government is asked to control practically everything, you have a socialist system, a system I do not favour because it always costs the government two or three times as much to run something people could run themselves.
It means that if the private sector is given a chance to offer those services, they are likely to be cheaper. We have the proof right here: it costs 25 per cent more in Canada than in the United States.
My question is this: If individuals and companies move to the United States because taxes are too high in this country, isn't it obvious that these services are costing us too much in terms of the way we are taxed in this country?

Madam Speaker, I am shocked to hear that comment by the hon. member from the Bloc Quebecois. I hope Quebecers come to know about this view that the health care system in Canada is a form of socialism which the hon. member rejects.
If you take the analysis that the hon. member has offered, that someone making $100,000 a year is able to get the same kind of health care in the United States and still have 25 per cent more disposable income I do not know whether that is true but let us say for the sake of argument that it is. The fact of the matter is that one of the reasons Canadians who are making $100,000 a year have less disposable income in this country is because

Government Orders
they are kicking in to a health care system through the tax system that provides health care for all Canadians in such a way that the person making $100,000 in the United States is not contributing to a health care system that would look after the 35 million Americans who do not have any health care insurance whatsoever.
From the perspective of somebody who makes $100,000 a year, the United States looks pretty good. That is to look at things only through the eyes of individuals and not to look at the common good or any notion of social justice or any notion of a country or anything else. It is this kind of small / liberal, individualistic analysis of reality that is getting us into all this trouble. I cannot get it through my thick head, as some would say, why people would decide to move to the United States simply because they could have a little more money. If that is all being a Canadian means to them, then good riddance.

Madam Speaker, my colleague from Eglinton-Lawrence and I have agreed to switch.
Before I came in this morning to speak on this bill, I had the occasion to talk to one of my friends on the Hill about a couple of mutual friends, Colin Sparling, a horse trainer from Sydney, Nova Scotia and Peter Berringer, a horse trainer from Aurora. We were talking about the lives of horse trainers in this country, people who get up every morning at five o'clock and have to muck out stalls and work in the cold. What relevance does this bill today have to the kind of life these people lead?
When one sees a document like this of nearly 2,000 pages one wonders how one begins to judge whether fairness exists. Before even judging fairness, one has to have the ability to understand. Like most people in this country, I cannot begin to ascertain truly whether this bill is fair.
We end up having blind faith in the bureaucrats who designed the words in this paper and hope that it achieves its end. That is why for the last two years I have been fighting hard in this House. We are getting more and more members realizing this. This week the Auditor General in his report said that the tax system, the tax designs and the tax forms of this country are not serving the clients.
We have to get back to simplicity because from simplicity we are going to begin the process of participation in a judgmental way as to what is happening in our tax system. Ultimately that is going to make all of us more accountable as politicians in this country for the taxes that we impose on our constituents from coast to coast to coast. I continue to flag that as a concern.
I want to go back to a remark made by the member for Winnipeg Transcona earlier today in answer to my question, when I asked him about the importance of using the tax system of this country to attract foreign capital. I happen to believe one of the most central problems we have in this country today is the flight of capital. The number of people fleeing this country with their capital because of the tax designs, whether individuals or corporations, is becoming a serious problem.
The New Democratic Party member for Winnipeg Transcona treated this issue rather lightly. I think he was being a little bit too defensive about the actions taken by the New Democratic government in the province of Ontario. I do not think it is linking the importance of capital to job creation.
The member said he did not want to make Canada a tax haven. I never said we should make Canada a tax haven, but I would not mind having international investors, local businessmen or local individuals who have accumulated wealth feeling this was a tax haven. I would not mind if every wealthy person in the world wanted to park their money in financial institutions in this country. I would much rather have the money here in financial institutions than in the islands or in Switzerland or in California where we have over one million Canadians right now. Many of them will say they are there because of our current tax act.
What is the importance of attracting that foreign capital to this country? Financial institutions only make money when they rent capital out. That is how our financial institutions make their money. When we have our financial institutions loaded with capital they compete with one another. The only way they can compete is through lower interest rates. That is what ultimately leads to job creation. When entrepreneurs can borrow money at 4 and 5 per cent and when banks have so much
December 5, 1991	COMMONS
capital that they want to push money out, that is when the entrepreneurial spirit of this country gets revitalized.
When the 900,000 entrepreneurs in this country have access to capital so that their creativity and their productivity can be exploited to the fullest, it creates jobs. That is how we lower the draw on our unemployment insurance fund. That is how we lower the draw on our welfare fund and that is how we attack the deficit and debt of this country.
I cannot understand why the government cannot see this issue. I cannot understand why it is not altering the tax designs of this country to attract foreign capital. The current tax designs are a disincentive to entrepreneurship. They are disincentives to productivity. I hear this from my constituents. I hear this from Canadians day in and day out. When is the Government of Canada going to do something to radically reform the tax system of this country so that it is fair? In order to get fairness, in order to judge fairness, you need simplicity and ultimately it will lead to efficiency.
Once again we have some minor amendments to the tax act of this country by Bill C-18. These minor amendments are close to 2,000 pages. As my colleague for Ottawa South and my colleague for Etobicoke North and many other colleagues in the Liberal Party are going to say throughout this debate, we must start giving Canadians some hope that we are going to finally change the tax act so that it is more simple and that it is more fair.
I want to go back to the capital flows that are so important in this country. For the last two to three weeks the Minister of Finance has been standing up and saying: "Interest rates have come down 5 to 6 per cent in the last eight months. Look at the way we are operating this economy".
Ask any entrepreneur in this country right now if it is easy to get capital to either maintain a business or to expand a business. Ask him if he can go to a bank and find out how it is treating its lines of credit. Ask how the banks in this country are treating new starters. Madam Speaker, if you can find more than 10 serious projects then I take my words back. I only hear from entrepreneurs. Whether they are people employing five or five thousand people, they say there is a serious shortage of credit in this country right now even though we have

interest rates that are the lowest they have been in 10 to 12 years. The reason why we have that problem is because we have a shortage of capital in this country. We have to do things to attract capital. We have to do things to stop the capital outflow from this country.
Someone could be making a million dollars a year. Someone could be an actor who makes $10 million a year. Why do we not change that tax design to keep that capital here so that capital can be used and rented out by financial institutions to entrepreneurs to do anything and everything from restaurants to auto parts, to service industries, to tourism, to whatever?
Why can we not do that? We can do that, Madam Speaker, if the government would just have the political will and listen to the people. The minister of trade just four weeks ago talked about consultation, consultation and consultation for competitiveness. If this government were serious about competitiveness-and I cannot believe it is not serious-it would listen to the person who is working on the shop floor and the person who is working in the office. They will tell you. They are not just telling me. I know other colleagues-even members of the government-are hearing people asking for some fairness in the tax designs of this country. That is the single most dramatic way to increase the productivity in this country. Productivity is ultimately what investors look for. That will attract foreign capital.
There has been a lack of political will to come up with a comprehensive approach to tax reform. I can remember the member for Welland-Grey-Dufferin-Simcoe heading up a task force on tax reform when he was in opposition. It was a good task force that went coast to coast listening to Canadians. And the government did say when it came in: "Phase I is tax reform". Madam Speaker, the government did not get into it deeply enough. It was amendments on top of amendments.
What Canadians are saying is to stop running the economy of Canada through the Department of Finance or through the tax system. There are so many rules, regulations, exceptions and exceptions to exceptions that we no longer understand how this tax act works. Use the tax instrument to collect revenue. When you want to do things in terms of social policy or in terms of aiding a specific sector, do it through direct program delivery through department by department. Do it in a way that

Government Orders
the people's money in this country can be accounted for rather than burying it in a 15,000-page tax act.
Madam Speaker, I believe that we are at a critical point in this country's future. The will of this country is fragile right now.

speechtext: I thank hon. members for their understanding of the situation. I know it must be difficult for the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood. There are five minutes remaining in his intervention.

Madam Speaker, we all wish our friend a speedy recovery.
As I was saying earlier I am trying to make this tax amendment, Bill C-18, relevant to my friends Colin Sparling and Peter Berringer.
I know and believe that if this government were to address comprehensive tax reform, if it were to send out a signal not only to the people of Canada but also to people around the world that we were going to come up with a tax design that met the test of efficiency and simplicity and fairness, just sending out that signal could change the spirit that exists within this economy. It could change that spirit almost overnight. It could just say it was going to do it in the February-March budget. If it just announced that now, I believe the recovery would begin.
This government must do something concrete to motivate Canadians, to turn on Canadians who at this time are in a state of almost chronic depression. They do not look to the provinces to do this. They look to their national government. They look to their national politicians.
When we have an opportunity like today in the House of Commons where we are talking about amendments to the tax act of this country, I think it is incumbent upon all of us to ask how this relates to the people in this country who are not tax lawyers and tax accountants and senior officials in the Department of Finance or the Department of National Revenue. How does the action we are taking today relate to the men and women of this country who are on the shop floor, who are in the back stretch, who are working in the restaurants, who are working in the hour-by-hour jobs? What will this act do to make their tax life more fair, more simple, more efficient?
This does not pass that test. Yes, there are some elements of modification in this bill that will improve fairness. However, it is tinkering; it is tampering. I was part of a government that did this as well. I am not exempting our track record on this, but it is time now for all of us to say that comprehensive tax reform is needed. The people of Canada are crying out for it, and we beg this Minister of Finance and this government to have the political will to do something by the next budget.

Madam Speaker, I have a few questions for the hon. member for Broadview- Greenwood. He says he was appalled at how much capital was leaving the country. He also said that we needed a better tax system or a complete overhaul of our tax structure. But I have yet to hear him say how he intends to improve our present tax system. My point is that Canada has a cumulative debt of $430 billion. That is not exactly peanuts. We have a cumulative debt of $430 million, with a population of not quite 27 million. The big problem facing us is that there are 11 political powers in Canada which are contradicting each other day after day. We have a striking example of what is going on now and driving up the debt.
We have a socialist government in Ontario now, in that province which accounts for 42 per cent of Canada's Gross Domestic Product, and its policies are completely opposite to those of the federal government. This inconsistency between these 11 governments leads to inefficiency, which is bankrupting us. Let us not try to find formulas. I think that the only formula that will help us understand, the only intelligent formula, is power to
December 5,1991	COMMONS DEBATES	5831
the provinces. Most provinces should have almost all the powers, as Quebec is asking for.
Madam Speaker, it is quite important because we are talking about the future of a country which is going broke. We must talk about it a little. The problem is that Quebec is rightly asking for at least 22 or 23 powers to be able to develop. On the other hand, the federal government wants to have all the powers. How much longer will this confrontation go on? Ten years, fifteen years, twenty years? This problem must be solved damn soon. Even if we came up with the best tax system in the world, we are still going broke day by day. For the past 20 years we have not been able to get the annual deficit below $30 billion. Something is not working there. The solution is a very high level of decentralization. We go even further than that, because English Canada does not understand. We say that we want Quebec to be a sovereign state. Maybe after that they will understand that we are right. Ontario will become sovereign, so will the west and the east, and then they may associate in some way. But the problem lies there.
